ctes.customer_spend:
SELECT
        o.CustomerID,
        COALESCE(c.FirstName || ' ' || c.LastName, 'Unknown') AS customer_name,
        SUM(o.Total_Order_Amount) AS total_spend
    FROM Orders AS o
    LEFT JOIN Customers AS c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
    GROUP BY o.CustomerID, c.FirstName, c.LastName
ctes.spend_with_avg:
SELECT
        cs.*,
        (SELECT AVG(total_spend) FROM customer_spend) AS avg_customer_spend
    FROM customer_spend AS cs

steps.title: Start with the orders
steps.change: `Orders` is the first `FROM` source because the report must retain each ordering customer’s purchase amount as the starting row before forming customer totals. It supplies both the customer ID and spend; order 10 contributes 300 for customer 1.

steps.title: Attach the customer names
steps.change: The left join preserves all three orders. Order 10 matches Asha Rao on ID 1. An unmatched customer ID would leave the name fields NULL.
steps.added_sql: LEFT JOIN Customers AS c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
steps.sql:
SELECT o.OrderID, o.CustomerID, o.Total_Order_Amount,
       c.CustomerID AS matched_customer_id, c.FirstName, c.LastName
FROM Orders AS o
LEFT JOIN Customers AS c ON o.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
ORDER BY o.OrderID;

steps.title: Sum each customer’s orders
steps.change: The `customer_spend` CTE is prepared from the original `Orders` and `Customers` tables, not from the preceding joined stage. `FROM Orders AS o` supplies every order amount; `LEFT JOIN Customers` on `CustomerID` adds names and keeps unmatched orders. `GROUP BY` produces one row per `CustomerID`/name group (including a `NULL`-ID group if present), so multiple orders contribute to one total. Order 10 contributes 300 for Asha.
steps.added_sql:
SUM(o.Total_Order_Amount) AS total_spend
-- one group per ordering ID and matched name
GROUP BY o.CustomerID, c.FirstName, c.LastName
steps.sql:
SELECT CustomerID, customer_name, total_spend
FROM customer_spend ORDER BY CustomerID;

steps.title: Attach the customer average
steps.change: `customer_spend` contains one row per `CustomerID`/name group, including a `NULL`-ID group if present. The outer `FROM customer_spend AS cs` starts from those totals; the scalar subquery reads all three sample totals (300 + 100 + 200) ÷ 3 = 200 and attaches that benchmark to every group. The locked query includes a `NULL`-ID group in the average, unlike the course answer.
steps.sql: SELECT * FROM spend_with_avg ORDER BY CustomerID;

steps.title: Filter to totals above the average
steps.change: Asha passes at 300 > 200. Ben's 100 falls below the benchmark. Cia equals 200, so the strict comparison removes her too.

steps.title: Calculate the percentage and sort
steps.change: Asha is 100 above the 200 average. Her percentage is 50.0. NULLIF guards the division and descending spend puts the highest qualifying total first.
steps.added_sql:
100.0 * (total_spend - avg_customer_spend)
    / NULLIF(avg_customer_spend, 0) AS pct_above_avg
-- final sort
ORDER BY total_spend DESC
